claim_1.claim: Flow cytometry analysis of heparinized whole blood from young adults (25–40 yo, n=15) and elderly adults (60–79 yo, n=21) at days 0, 1, 3, 7, 14, 28, 90 and 180 post-vaccination showed significant CD4+ T cell responses after Zostavax® compared to baseline (day 0).

sources.quote: In contrast significant CD4+ T cell responses were detected in the majority of subjects (Figure 1B), consistent with a recent report (Qi et al., 2016).

Figure 1. Zostavax® study overview, cellular and antibody responses B) CD8+ and CD4+ T cell activation as measured by Ki67+Bcl2- in young adults (black, n=13 for CD8+, n=15 for CD4+) and the elderly (orange, n=19 for CD8+, n=21 for CD4+). Mean values in solid lines, and shades for 90% confidence interval.

claim_2.claim: Flow cytometry analysis of cryopreserved PBMCs from young adults (25–40 yo, n=16) and elderly adults (60–79 yo, n=20) at days 0, 1, 3, 7, 14, 28, 90 and 180 post-vaccination showed increased CD4+CXCR5+CXCR3+ICOS+ Tfh-like cells after Zostavax® in both age groups compared to baseline (day 0).

sources.quote: Figure 1C shows an increase in CD4+CXCR5+CXCR3+ICOS+ T cells after Zostavax® in both the young and elderly adults.
Figure 1. Zostavax® study overview, cellular and antibody responses C) Increase in VZV-specific Tfh-like cells (as measured by CXCR5+ICOS+CXCR3+) in young adults (n=16) and the elderly (n=20).

claim_3.claim: ELISPOT analysis of PBMCs from young adults (25–40 yo, n=17) and elderly adults (60–79 yo, n=22) at days 0, 1, 3, 7, 14, 28, 90 and 180 post-vaccination showed increased antigen-specific IFN-γ, IL-4, and IL-21 production by CD4+ T cells after Zostavax® compared to baseline (day 0).

sources.quote: Significant increase in CD4+ T cells that are positive for IFN-γ, IL-4 and IL-21 were also detected, indicating a mixed Th1/Th2/Th21 profile (Figure 1C).

Figure 1. Zostavax® study overview, cellular and antibody responses C) Increase in VZV-specific Tfh-like cells (as measured by CXCR5+ICOS+CXCR3+) in young adults (n=16) and the elderly (n=20). Antigen-specific IFN-γ, IL-4 or IL-21 production by CD4+ T cells as measured by ELISPOT in young adults (n=17) and the elderly (n=22). SFC = Spot forming cells.

claim_5.claim: ELISPOT analysis of PBMCs from a subset of HLA-A2+ individuals (n=13) at days 0, 1, 3, 7, 14, 28, 90 and 180 post-vaccination showed no CD8+ T cell response to VZV HLA-A2-restricted vaccine peptides in most subjects after vaccination compared to baseline (day 0).

sources.quote: Despite detectable VZV-specific CD8+ T cell responses at baseline, the CD8+ T cells did not respond to the vaccine peptides with the exception of two individuals (ZV113 and ZV118, Figure 1D).

Figure 1. Zostavax® study overview, cellular and antibody responses D) Antigen-specific CD8+ T cell responses and Zostavax DNAemia in a subset of HLA-A2+ individuals (n=13). PBMCs stimulated with previously published VZV-HLA-A2 restricted peptides overnight and IFN-γ measured via ELISPOT. Viral DNA copies in blood measured by PCR

claim_7.claim: ELISPOT analysis of PBMCs from young adults (25–40 yo, n=5) and elderly adults (60–79 yo, n=8) at days 0, 1, 3, 7, 14, 28, 90 and 180 post-vaccination showed a transient peak of Zostavax®-specific plasmablast cells 7 days after vaccination (day 7) compared to days 0, 14, 28, 90 and 180.

sources.quote: We detected a transient peak of antigen-specific plasmablast cells 7 days after Zostavax® administration (Figure 1E), consistent with the plasmablast responses observed to other vaccines such as influenza (Wrammert et al., 2008).
Figure 1. Zostavax® study overview, cellular and antibody responses E) Representative VZV-specific IgG ELISPOT. Number of Zostavax®-specific plasmablasts in young adults (n=5) and the elderly (n=8).

claim_9.claim: ELISA analysis of plasma from young adults (25–40 yo, n=16) at days 0, 1, 3, 7, 14, 28, 90 and 180 post-vaccination showed significant increases in VZV glycoprotein-specific IgG induced by Zostavax® compared to baseline (day 0).

sources.quote: The measurement of VZV glycoprotein-specific IgG over the course of the study showed significant increases induced by Zostavax® in both the young and elderly adults (Figure 1E).

Figure 1. Zostavax® study overview, cellular and antibody responses E) Representative VZV-specific IgG ELISPOT. Number of Zostavax®-specific plasmablasts in young adults (n=5) and the elderly (n=8). Kinetic analysis of Zostavax® glycoprotein-specific IgG antibodies as measured by ELISA in young adults (n=16) and the elderly (n=21).

claim_10.claim: ELISA analysis of plasma from elderly adults (60–79 yo, n=21) at days 0, 1, 3, 7, 14, 28, 90 and 180 post-vaccination showed significant increases in VZV glycoprotein-specific IgG induced by Zostavax® compared to baseline (day 0).

sources.quote: The measurement of VZV glycoprotein-specific IgG over the course of the study showed significant increases induced by Zostavax® in both the young and elderly adults (Figure 1E).

Figure 1. Zostavax® study overview, cellular and antibody responses E) Representative VZV-specific IgG ELISPOT. Number of Zostavax®-specific plasmablasts in young adults (n=5) and the elderly (n=8). Kinetic analysis of Zostavax® glycoprotein-specific IgG antibodies as measured by ELISA in young adults (n=16) and the elderly (n=21).

claim_11.claim: ELISA analysis of plasma from young adults (25–40 yo, n=16) and elderly adults (60–79 yo, n=21) at days 0, 1, 3, 7, 14, 28, 90 and 180 post-vaccination showed that VZV glycoprotein-specific IgG peaked between two and four weeks after vaccination (days 14 and 28) compared to days 0, 1, 3, 7, 90 and 180.

sources.quote: The IgG antibody peaked between two and four weeks after vaccination, and dropped by 180 days after vaccination.

Figure 1. Zostavax® study overview, cellular and antibody responses E) Representative VZV-specific IgG ELISPOT. Number of Zostavax®-specific plasmablasts in young adults (n=5) and the elderly (n=8). Kinetic analysis of Zostavax® glycoprotein-specific IgG antibodies as measured by ELISA in young adults (n=16) and the elderly (n=21).

claim_15.claim: Human U133 Plus 2.0 Arrays analysis of PBMCs from vaccinees at day 1 and day 3 post-vaccination showed that interferon induced antiviral genes MX1 and IFI44L and the phosphoserine phosphatase PSPH were highly upregulated compared to baseline (day 0).

sources.quote: Besides the interferon induced antiviral genes, such as MX1 and IFI44L, a phosphoserine phosphatase, PSPH, was highly upregulated at day 1/0 and day 3/0 (Figure S2A).

claim_16.claim: Human U133 Plus 2.0 Arrays analysis of PBMCs from vaccinees at day 7 post-vaccination showed that immunoglobulin genes, TNFRSF17, and MZB1 were highly upregulated compared to baseline (day 0).

sources.quote: At day 7, immunoglobulin genes were highly upregulated, as well as TNFRSF17 and MZB1, two genes extensively reported for their roles in antibody production (Li et al., 2014; Nakaya et al., 2011; Querec et al., 2009) (Figure S2A).

claim_17.claim: Human U133 Plus 2.0 Arrays analysis of PBMCs from vaccinees, using blood transcription modules, at day 7 post-vaccination showed a strong plasmablast signature compared to baseline (day 0).

sources.quote: BTM analysis of the response to Zostavax® revealed signatures seen with several other vaccines, including the seasonal influenza vaccines and the meningococcal vaccine such as a strong plasmablast signature at day 7 (Figure S2B), consistent with the robust plasmablast response at this time point (Figure 1E).

claim_18.claim: Human U133 Plus 2.0 Arrays analysis of PBMCs from vaccinees, using blood transcription modules, showed weaker induction of innate immunity modules related to antigen presentation, dendritic cells, cytosolic DNA sensing, RIG-I receptor signaling, and type I IFN responses after Zostavax® compared to YF-17D.

sources.quote: Surprisingly however, several BTMs related to innate immunity including those relating to antigen presentation, dendritic cells, antiviral innate immune sensing including cytosolic DNA sensing, RIG-I receptor signaling and type I IFN responses were weakly induced by Zostavax® relative to YF-17D, which is another live viral vector (Figure S2B).

claim_23.claim: High-resolution metabolomics analysis of plasma from vaccinees at days 0, 1, 3, 7 and 14 post-vaccination showed the largest numbers of differential metabolites at day 1 and day 14 compared to baseline (day 0).

sources.quote: Compared to the baseline, both negative and positive ionization data indicated the largest numbers of differential metabolites at day 1 and day 14 (under negative ionization, 429 and 425 peaks at FDR < 0.1, respectively).

claim_24.claim: High-resolution metabolomics analysis of plasma from vaccinees at day 1 post-vaccination showed that day 1/0 significant metabolite peaks had little overlap with chemicals in the vaccine compared to vaccine-derived peaks.

sources.quote: Few overlap peaks were found between the day 1/0 significant metabolite peaks and chemicals in the vaccine (data not shown), indicating that the human metabolomic changes were not simply due to carryover from chemicals in the vaccine.

claim_25.claim: High-resolution metabolomics analysis of plasma from vaccinees at day 1 post-vaccination, using mummichog pathway analysis, showed enrichment of TCA cycle, glycolysis and gluconeogenesis, and propanoate metabolism compared to baseline (day 0).

sources.quote: We used the mummichog software, a pathway tool designed for untargeted metabolomics data (Li et al., 2013), to evaluate the day 1/0 significant metabolic pathways shown in Figure 2C. Strikingly, TCA cycle (and overlapping glycolysis and gluconeogenesis) and propanoate metabolism was also identified in the day 3/0 transcriptomics data (Table S3).

Figure 2. Plasma metabolomics and association with PBMC transcriptomics after Zostavax® vaccination C) Significantly enriched pathways for Day 1 vs Day 0 (both negative and positive ionization), by the mummichog software (Li et al., 2013).

claim_39.claim: Human U133 Plus 2.0 Arrays analysis of PBMCs from young adults (25–40 years) and elderly adults (60–79 years) at baseline (day 0) showed higher inflammation, cytosolic DNA sensing, and NK cell gene modules in the elderly group compared to the young group.

sources.quote: The most significant gene network consisted of gene modules related to inflammation, cytosolic DNA sensing and NK cells, which were significantly higher in the elderly group (Figure 4B), consistent with our recent results(Nakaya et al., 2015).

Figure 4. Age difference explained by MMRN A) The subnetwork from MMRN related to age groups, colored by t-score in comparison between the young and elderly groups. Red indicates higher value in elderly. The most significant gene network is shown in B) and C), cytokine network in D).

claim_40.claim: Human U133 Plus 2.0 Arrays analysis of PBMCs from young adults (25–40 years) and elderly adults (60–79 years) at baseline (day 0) showed lower IL7R expression in the elderly group compared to the young group.

sources.quote: Interestingly, there was lower expression level of IL7R gene in the elderly group (Figure 4C, by red arrow), suggesting a potential compensatory mechanism.

Figure 4. Age difference explained by MMRN A) The subnetwork from MMRN related to age groups, colored by t-score in comparison between the young and elderly groups. Red indicates higher value in elderly. The most significant gene network is shown in B) and C), cytokine network in D). In C), each column represents a subject at day 0, colored by z-scores of gene expression values. IL7R is marked by a red arrow.

claim_41.claim: Flow cytometry analysis of PBMCs from young adults (25–40 years) and elderly adults (60–79 years) at baseline (day 0) showed higher NK cell frequencies in the elderly group compared to the young group.

sources.quote: Furthermore, difference in NK cells measured by flow cytometry (Figure 4E) was consistent with the transcriptomics data, and Luminex data supported the higher level of IL-7 in the elderly group (Figure 4F).
Figure 4. Age difference explained by MMRN E) Baseline NK cell frequencies measured by flow cytometry.

claim_42.claim: Luminex analysis of plasma from young adults (25–40 years) and elderly adults (60–79 years) at day 3 post-vaccination showed higher IL-7 levels in the elderly group compared to the young group.

sources.quote: Furthermore, difference in NK cells measured by flow cytometry (Figure 4E) was consistent with the transcriptomics data, and Luminex data supported the higher level of IL-7 in the elderly group (Figure 4F).
Figure 4. Age difference explained by MMRN F) Day 3/0 IL-7 levels measured by Luminex.

claim_43.claim: Human U133 Plus 2.0 Arrays analysis of PBMCs from females and males at day 3 post-vaccination showed higher activity of many T cell related gene modules in females compared to males.

sources.quote: In stark contrast to the age network, the sex related network shows the majority of activities that were higher in females at day 3/0 (Figure S6C), with many T cell related gene modules (Figure S6D).

claim_44.claim: Human U133 Plus 2.0 Arrays analysis of PBMCs from PCR+ and PCR− vaccinees showed higher baseline plasma cell signature genes, BCR signaling, heme biosynthesis, and inositol phosphate metabolism in the PCR+ group compared to the PCR− group.

sources.quote: The PCR+ group had higher baseline levels of plasma cells signature genes and BCR signaling, although these signatures were unlikely to have derived from VZV specific plasmablasts; they also had higher gene expression for heme biosynthesis and inositol phosphate metabolism (Figure S6E).

claim_45.claim: Human U133 Plus 2.0 Arrays analysis of PBMCs from PCR+ and PCR− vaccinees at day 7 post-vaccination showed higher cytoskeleton remodeling, cell adhesion, platelet activation, and G protein mediated calcium signaling in the PCR+ group compared to the PCR− group.

sources.quote: By day 7/0, the PCR+ group had higher activity in cytoskeleton remodeling (enriched for SRF targets), cell adhesion, platelet activation and G protein mediated calcium signaling (Figure S6E), possibly indicative of a response to viral replication.

claim_46.claim: Human U133 Plus 2.0 Arrays analysis of PBMCs from PCR+ and PCR− vaccinees at day 7 post-vaccination showed lower plasma cell signature genes in the PCR+ group compared to the PCR− group.

sources.quote: The PCR+ group also had lower activity in plasma cells signature genes at day 7/0 (Figure S6F), indicating a compromised antibody response.

claim_47.claim: Luminex analysis of plasma from PCR+ and PCR− vaccinees at day 7 post-vaccination showed higher RANTES in the PCR− group compared to the PCR+ group.

sources.quote: Interestingly, the day 7/0 cytokine RANTES is significantly higher in the PCR− group (Figure S6F).

claim_59.claim: High-resolution metabolomics analysis of plasma from vaccinees at day 1 post-vaccination showed significant changes in metabolites related to inositol phosphate metabolism compared to baseline (day 0).

sources.quote: Metabolites related to this pathway were significantly changed 1 day after vaccination (Figure 2C), and were extensively associated with gene signatures (Figure 3).

Figure 2. Plasma metabolomics and association with PBMC transcriptomics after Zostavax® vaccination C) Significantly enriched pathways for Day 1 vs Day 0 (both negative and positive ionization), by the mummichog software (Li et al., 2013).

claim_60.claim: Human U133 Plus 2.0 Arrays analysis of PBMCs from vaccinees at day 7 post-vaccination showed that BCR signaling, phosphatidylinositol signaling, and inositol phosphate metabolism explained more transcriptomic variance than most other data types compared to lower-ranked contributors.

sources.quote: Indeed, when we examined the contributing factors to the day 7/0 transcriptome by variance analysis (Nath et al., 2012), BCR signaling, phosphatidylinositol signaling and inositol phosphate metabolism were on the top of the list, besides house-keeping genes such as mRNA processing (Figure 7A).

Figure 7. Immune phenotyping by inositol phosphate metabolism A) Percent of variance in the day 7/0 transcriptome explained by each data types, using weighted average of the variance captured by the first five principal components (Nath et al., 2012).

claim_62.claim: Human U133 Plus 2.0 Arrays analysis of PBMCs from vaccinees across days 0, 1, 3 and 7 showed that subjects with hyper-PSPH activity clustered within the high inositol phosphate metabolism group compared to the low inositol phosphate metabolism group.

sources.quote: Combining data from all time points, groups of subjects of low or high IP metabolism emerged from unsupervised clustering (Figure 7D). Interestingly, all the subjects with hyper-PSPH activity fall into the H5 cluster of high IP metabolism (Figure 7D).

Figure 7. Immune phenotyping by inositol phosphate metabolism D) Hierarchical clustering of subjects based on their gene expression of IP metabolism (M129). The clusters are color coded in the same way as for E–F). The expression of plasma cell signature genes (M156.1) is shown in the two heat maps on the bottom. Each column corresponds to a subject, matched in all three heat maps. The outliers in C are colored in orange, shown to the top of gene heat maps.

claim_63.claim: Human U133 Plus 2.0 Arrays analysis of PBMCs from low and high inositol phosphate metabolism subject groups showed higher expression of plasma cell signature genes at day 1 in the high inositol phosphate metabolism group compared to the low group.

sources.quote: This pattern in IP metabolism penetrated into the expression of plasma cell signature genes (M156.1), whereas the group of high IP metabolism showed high expression of immunoglobulins at day 1/0, but low expression at day 7/0 (Figure 7D–E).

Figure 7. Immune phenotyping by inositol phosphate metabolism D) Hierarchical clustering of subjects based on their gene expression of IP metabolism (M129). The clusters are color coded in the same way as for E–F). The expression of plasma cell signature genes (M156.1) is shown in the two heat maps on the bottom. Each column corresponds to a subject, matched in all three heat maps. The outliers in C are colored in orange, shown to the top of gene heat maps. E–F) Boxplots for the clusters in D). The p-values are given by Student’s t-test comparing clusters L2 (low) and H5 (high in IP metabolism).

sources.quote: This pattern in IP metabolism penetrated into the expression of plasma cell signature genes (M156.1), whereas the group of high IP metabolism showed high expression of immunoglobulins at day 1/0, but low expression at day 7/0 (Figure 7D–E).

claim_65.claim: ELISA analysis of plasma from low and high inositol phosphate metabolism subject groups at day 28 post-vaccination showed no significant difference in Zostavax®-specific IgG between the groups.

sources.quote: The Zostavax® specific IgG at day 28/0 followed a similar pattern as day 7/0 M156.1, but the difference between subject groups did not reach statistical significance (Figure 7E).

Figure 7. Immune phenotyping by inositol phosphate metabolism E–F) Boxplots for the clusters in D). The p-values are given by Student’s t-test comparing clusters L2 (low) and H5 (high in IP metabolism).

claim_66.claim: Flow cytometry analysis of PBMCs from low and high inositol phosphate metabolism subject groups showed significantly lower numbers of activated CD4+ T cells in the high inositol phosphate metabolism group compared to the low group.

sources.quote: Similarly, the group of high IP metabolism had significantly lower number of activated CD4+ T cells (Figure 7F).

Figure 7. Immune phenotyping by inositol phosphate metabolism E–F) Boxplots for the clusters in D). The p-values are given by Student’s t-test comparing clusters L2 (low) and H5 (high in IP metabolism).

claim_67.claim: High-resolution metabolomics analysis of plasma from low and high inositol phosphate metabolism subject groups showed lower levels of metabolite cluster Neg257, tentatively matched to glycerophospholipids, in the high inositol phosphate metabolism group compared to the low group.

sources.quote: Lower level of plasma metabolite cluster Neg257, which is tentatively matched to glycerophospholipids, was also seen in this group, together with differences in neutrophils and cytokines (Figure 7F).

Figure 7. Immune phenotyping by inositol phosphate metabolism E–F) Boxplots for the clusters in D). The p-values are given by Student’s t-test comparing clusters L2 (low) and H5 (high in IP metabolism).

claim_68.claim: Human U133 Plus 2.0 Arrays analysis of PBMCs from vaccinees showed that high inositol phosphate metabolism was detrimental to both T cell and B cell responses compared to low inositol phosphate metabolism.

sources.quote: These data suggest that high activity in IP metabolism was detrimental to both T cell and B cell responses.
